text: Full Electronic Registration (e-Registration) now available on the ePortal | In a major boost to capital market regulation in Nigeria, President Ahmed Bola Tinubu GCFR, has assented to the Investments and Securities Bill (ISB) 2025, which repeals the Investments and Securities Act No. 29 of 2007 | Full Electronic Registration (e-Registration) now available on the ePortal | In a major boost to capital market regulation in Nigeria, President Ahmed Bola Tinubu GCFR, has assented to the Investments and Securities Bill (ISB) 2025, which repeals the Investments and Securities Act No. 29 of 2007 | Become an Operator Published: September 4, 2023 Are you a business in Nigeria interested in becoming a capital market operator (CMO)? Our meticulous checklist ensures you cover every essential requirement, leaving no room for compliance gaps. Here is a step-by-step guide to the registration process, as well as the requirements for each type of CMO. Step 1: Register your Business with the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC) Section 38(2) of the Companies and Allied Matters Act (CAMA) 2020 requires all companies to be registered with the CAC, therefore all businesses in Nigeria must be registered with the CAC before they can apply for registration as a CMO. To register your business with the CAC, you will need to: Create an account on the CAC website . Select the type of company you want to register. Complete the online registration form and pay the required fees. Submit your application and supporting documents. Once your application is approved, you will receive a Certificate of Incorporation. For more details on CAC registration for businesses, see this guide curated for you. Step 2: Choose a Type of Capital Market Operator (CMO) Section 10 of the Investment and Securities Act (ISA) 2007 defines a capital market operator as "any person who engages in the business of dealing in securities or provides services in relation to securities." If this is indeed the type of business dealing you wish to go into, it is important to note that there are different types of CMOs in Nigeria, each with its own specific functions and requirements. Some of the most common types of CMOs in Nigeria include: Brokers: Act as intermediaries between buyers and sellers of securities. Broker/Dealers: Buy and sell securities on behalf of clients and for their own account. Central System Depositories: Hold securities in electronic form and facilitate the transfer of ownership of securities. Corporate Investment Advisers: Provide investment advice to corporate clients. Corporate Sub-Brokers: Act as intermediaries between brokers and their clients. Custodians: Hold securities in safekeeping for clients. Dealers: Buy and sell securities for their own account. Estate Surveyors/Valuers: Value property for the purposes of issuing securities. Floor Brokers : Facilitate the trading of securities on a trading floor. Floor Traders: Trade securities on their own account on a trading floor. FMDQ OTC Dealers: Trade securities over the counter on the FMDQ OTC Securities Exchange. Fund/Portfolio Managers: Manage investment funds on behalf of clients. Individual Sub-Brokers: Act as intermediaries between brokers and their individual clients. Inter-Dealer Brokers: Facilitate the trading of securities between dealers. Investment Advisers: Provide investment advice to clients. Issuing Houses: Assist companies with the issuance of securities. Market Makers: Maintain a bid-ask spread for securities to ensure liquidity in the market. Over-the-Counter Exchanges: Facilitate the trading of securities outside of a trading floor. Portfolio Managers: Manage investment portfolios on behalf of clients. Property Managers: Manage property on behalf of clients. Private Equity Fund Managers: Manage private equity funds on behalf of investors. Rating Agencies: Assess the creditworthiness of issuers of securities. Receiving Bankers: Receive and manage subscription funds for new issues of securities. Registrars: Keep track of the ownership of securities. Reporting Accountant/Auditor: Prepare and audit the financial statements of public companies. Securities Lending Agents: Facilitate the lending and borrowing of securities. Self-Regulatory Organizations (SROs): Non-governmental organizations that develop rules that promote fair and orderly trading, protects investors, and maintains high standards of conduct among market participants. Solicitors: Provide legal advice on capital market transactions. Sub-Brokers: Act as intermediaries between brokers and their clients. Trustees: Hold assets in trust for the benefit of others. Underwriters: Guarantee to buy any securities that are not sold to investors in a new issue. Venture Capital Managers: Manage venture capital funds on behalf of investors. Commodity Brokers: Intermediaries between buyers and sellers of commodity contracts, facilitating trades on behalf of clients for a commission. They do not own the underlying commodities themselves. Commodity Dealers: Buy and sell commodity contracts for their own account, aiming to profit from price fluctuations. They act as market makers, providing liquidity and influencing prices. Commodity Broker-Dealers: Combine the functions of a broker and a dealer. They execute trades for clients while also engaging in proprietary trading activities in the same commodity market. Step 3: Meet the Registration Requirements for the Chosen Type of CMO Section 11 of the ISA 2007 sets out the general registration requirements for CMOs. These requirements include: Having a minimum capital requirement, which is set by the SEC in its Rules and Regulations. The minimum capital requirements for CMOs in Nigeria vary depending on the type of CMO. Find the Minimum Capital Requirement for each CMO Having directors and officers who are fit and proper to perform the functions of a CMO. These directors must be honest, trustworthy, and competent. Whether you are an aspiring entrepreneur seeking initial capital or an established company looking to expand, the SEC is here to empower you with the knowledge and resources to achieve your financial goals. Understanding Your Funding Needs The first step in your capital raising journey is to clearly define your funding requirements. Assess your current financial situation, identify your short-term and long-term goals, and determine the specific amount of capital needed to achieve those goals. This exercise will help you tailor your capital-raising strategy to the most suitable financing options. Exploring the Capital Markets Landscape The Nigerian capital markets offer a diverse range of financing solutions to cater to the varying needs of businesses and governments. Familiarize yourself with the different types of securities available, such as equity, debt, and hybrid securities, and understand the advantages and limitations of each. Navigating the Regulatory Framework The SEC plays a crucial role in ensuring a fair and transparent capital market environment. As you explore various financing options, it is essential to adhere to the SEC's regulations and guidelines to safeguard your interests and protect investors' rights. Engaging with Capital Market Intermediaries Capital market intermediaries, such as investment banks, stockbrokers, and solicitors, can provide valuable expertise and guidance throughout your capital-raising process. These intermediaries can assist you in structuring your offerings, conducting due diligence, and connecting you with potential investors. Exploring Alternative Funding Options In addition to traditional capital market instruments, consider alternative funding sources such as venture capitalists, and crowdfunding platforms. These alternative options may be particularly attractive for early-stage businesses or those with innovative business models. Capital Raising Process: A Step-by-Step Guide Develop a Compelling Business Plan: Create a comprehensive business plan that clearly outlines your business strategy, financial projections, and target market. This plan will serve as your roadmap for attracting investors' interest. Conduct Thorough Market Research: Analyze your industry, competitors, and target market to understand the prevailing market conditions, investor preferences, and potential risks. This research will inform your capital raising strategy and positioning. Structure Your Offering: Choose the most suitable type of security for your capital raising needs, whether it's equity, debt, or a hybrid instrument. Consider factors such as ownership dilution, interest payments, and dilution of voting rights. You can have a look at our repository of executed transactions to serve as templates for this step Prepare Offering Documents: Compile the necessary documentation, including a prospectus, financial statements, and risk factors disclosure, to provide investors with a comprehensive understanding of your business and the investment opportunity. You can look at our requirements for registration of securities to serve as a requirements checklist for this step. Engage with Capital Market Intermediaries: Select investment banks, stockbrokers, solicitors and other relevant market intermediaries with a good regulatory standing with the Commission to assist you in structuring your offering, conducting due diligence, and marketing your investment opportunity to potential investors. You can search for a registered operator here to get you started on this step. Comply with SEC Regulations: Adhere strictly to the SEC's regulations governing securities offerings, ensuring that all disclosures are fully made, accurate and transparent to protect investors' interests. Engage in Investor Roadshows: Present your business plan and investment opportunity to potential investors through roadshows, meetings, and conferences. Effectively communicate your value proposition and address investors' concerns. Negotiate Terms and Conditions: Negotiate the terms and conditions of the investment deal with potential investors, balancing your capital needs with the desired equity dilution or interest rates. Close the Deal: Once you have reached an agreement with investors, complete the necessary documentation and finalize the transaction. Maintain Transparency and Compliance: Continuously disclose material information to investors and comply with ongoing SEC reporting requirements to maintain investor confidence and trust. text: Close Home Exclusives Recapitalization Financial Analysis Corporate Stories Interviews Investigations Metrics Nairalytics Economy Business News Budget Public Debt Tax Markets Currencies Cryptos Commodities Equities Fixed Income Funds Management Securities Sectors Agriculture Aviation Company News Consumer Goods Corporate Updates Corporate deals Corporate Press Releases Energy Entertainment Financial Services Health Hospitality & Travel Manufacturing Real Estate and Construction Renewables & Sustainability Tech News Financial Literacy Career tips Personal Finance Lifestyle Billionaire Watch Profiles Opinions Blurb Market Views Op-Eds Research Analysis Search Business July 19, 2023 Transcorp Plc announces resignation of CFO, Joseph Adegunwa Transcorp Plc has announced the resignation of Mr Joseph Adegunwa from his role as Group CFO with effect from Friday, July 14th 2023. Nathanael Disu 2 min read Follow Us on Google Discover Joseph Adegunwa Transcorp Plc has announced the resignation of Mr Joseph Adegunwa from his role as Group Chief Financial Officer with effect from Friday, July 14 th 2023. This is according to a statement signed by the Acting Group Company Secretary, Funmi Olofintuyi and filed with the Nigerian Exchange Limited (NGX) on Tuesday, July 18 th 2023. Excerpts of the press release read: “We write to formally notify the Nigerian Exchange Limited and the investing public of the resignation of the Group Chief Finance Officer (GCFO) of Transnational Corporation Plc, Mr Joseph Adegunwa, with effect from Friday, July 14, 2023.’’ Mr Joseph Adegunwa’s resignation comes less than 2 years after his appointment as CFO. Also Read Warren Buffett steps down as Berkshire Hathaway chairman after 60 years Nigeria repatriates Chinese fugitive arrested in Ogun over ¥15.7 million rosewood smuggling Canada raises study permit, visitor visa processing times for Nigerians Profile of Mr Joseph Adegunwa Joseph Adegunwa is an astute finance expert with experience in Finance, Audit, Advisory, Strategy and Investment Management. He has worked in different sectors including but not limited to banking, real estate, advisory and investment management, among others. Joseph is an alumnus of the Lagos State University where he obtained a degree in Accounting (Second Class Upper Division). He is a fellow of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of Nigeria (ICAN) and a member of the Chartered Institute of Management Accountants (CIMA). About Transcorp Transnational Corporation of Nigeria Plc (Transcorp) is a publicly listed conglomerate, with a diversified shareholder base of about 300,000. It has diversified business interests that cut across the power, hospitality, and oil and gas sectors. Some of its portfolio include; Transcorp Hilton Abuja, Transcorp Hotels Calabar, Transcorp Power Ltd, Trans-Afam Power Ltd, Transcorp Energy and digital hospitality platform, Aura by Transcorp Hotels. What you should know Transcorp Plc in the first quarter (Q1), of 2023 declared N32.39 billion in revenue, representing an increase of 3.30% from N31.39 billion in Q1 2022. The increase in revenue was primarily driven by N24.14 billion generated from Power, followed by N8.25 billion from Hospitality in the period under review. Transcorp’s Profit Before Tax (PBT) also fell by 50.18% to N2.85 billion in Q1 2023 from N5.73 billion in the first quarter of 2022. title: Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention
text: Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention Protecting the health of Nigerians Archive Months Weeks Recent Publication Advanced NFETP FAQ Saturday, April 10, 2021 Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) What is Advanced NFETP? To address the different levels of expertise required at the national, state and local government levels, the NFETP is being implemented as a three-tiered pyramidal model: the Integrated Training for Surveillance Officers in Nigeria (ITSON), the Intermediate NFETP (I-NFETP) and the Advanced NFETP (A-NFETP) The Advanced Nigeria Field Epidemiology Training Programme (NFETP) is a two-year in-service training programme which provides competency-based training and service delivery in applied epidemiology and public health. It is coordinated by the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control (NCDC) in collaboration with the Federal Ministry of Health (FMoH), Federal Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development (FMARD) and Federal Ministry of Environment (FMEnv). The programme aims to build workforce capacity in disease surveillance and response, with dedicated mentorship using the One Health approach. The trainees support and contribute to the growth of public health capacity at national and state levels during the training and gain practical experience through field placements. Is the NFETP an accredited programme? Yes. The NFETP was accredited by the Global Accreditation Body of Training Programs in Epidemiology and Public Health Interventions Network (TEPHINET) in 2018. How does NFETP help the country? • Residents and graduates of the NFETP are trained with skills required to prevent, prepare for, rapidly detect and respond to disease outbreaks and public health threats. • They enhance the country’s public health workforce, contributing to national and global health security. What impact has the NFETP had on the country? NFETP residents and graduates have responded to a range of outbreaks both within the country and internationally. The outbreaks responded to include communicable diseases such as viral haemorrhagic fevers, meningitis, cholera and COVID-19 as well as environmental hazards such as lead poisoning. What are the programme objectives? To train future leaders in applied epidemiology using a solutions-based approach to public health events. To provide epidemiological capacity as part of Nigeria?s health security To strengthen public health surveillance systems for human, animal, and environmental health. To strengthen the One Health approach to outbreak preparedness and response, including the linkage between public health, veterinary public health, and environmental health. To develop capacity that will contribute effectively to public health research activities for human, animal and environmental health. To improve communications and networking among public health practitioners and researchers in Nigeria and across African countries. To strengthen affiliations with international organisations, such as the Training Programmes in Epidemiology and Public Health Interventions Network (TEPHINET), AFENET and other applied epidemiology and laboratory training programmes. What is the plan of work and timeline for NFETP? • It is a full-time two-year in-service training programme in field epidemiology that provides competency based training and service delivery in applied epidemiology and public health. • It is 70% field based and 30% classroom based. Is there any oversight committee for the programme? Yes. The Advisory Board which is chaired by the Honourable Minister of Health will provide oversight for the programme to ensure it meets its objectives. The Implementation Committee chaired by the Director General of NCDC will provide oversight for day-to-day operations of the programme Where is the management of the programme located? The NCDC as the National Public Health Institute (NPHI) in Nigeria has the mandate as contained in the NCDC Act, to lead the coordination of the NFETP with support from partners. What skills will be expected from the graduate? It is expected that an NFETP graduate will acquire the following skills: Epidemiological Methods Biostatistics Public Health Surveillance Laboratory and Biostatistics Communication Computer Technology Management and Leadership Prevention effectiveness Teaching and Mentoring Epidemiology of priority diseases and injuries What certification will the graduates of the NFETP receive? Graduates will be given a final certificate signed by the NCDC DG. How will the training be conducted? • Training is largely practical and field-based. • It is divided into 70% field work and 30% class work (didactic component), with the latter conducted in Abuja. What is the maximum number of candidates the NFETP recruit? The number of candidates is limited to some factors including the availability of funding, priority field placements, space for training, size of the recruiting pool and availability of career opportunities. What are the career opportunities for graduates of NFETP? These include: • Locally: - Epidemiologist (e.g., in national disease prevention and control programmes or State Ministry of Health) - Programme Manager (e.g., in national disease control programmes) • Internationally: - Non-Governmental Organisations (NGOs) with public health functions How is the NFETP funded? The programme is currently funded by the Government of Nigeria, with support from the World Bank through the Regional Disease Surveillance Systems Enhancement (REDISSE) project. It is also supported by partners. Do I need to pay for the programme? The programme is currently fully funded, and residents will be provided with stipends to support them while on the programme. Can I work during the programme? The programme is full-time, so, a letter of release from your or workplace is required. Who is qualified/eligible to apply? To apply for this fellowship, you must have: A Master of Public Health (MPH) degree or Masters? degree (MSc) in epidemiology, statistics,

title: Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention
text: Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention Protecting the health of Nigerians Archive Months Weeks Recent Publication 2019 Field Epidemiology and Laboratory Training Program, Cohort 11, Ahmadu Bello University Monday, April 01, 2019 AHMADU BELLO UNIVERSITY in collaboration with FEDERAL MINISTRY OF HEALTH and FEDERAL MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE AND RURAL DEVELOPMENT announces the 2019 Field Epidemiology and Laboratory Training Program for the award of A. MPH in Field Epidemiology, B. MPH in Veterinary Epidemiology & C. MPH in Laboratory Epidemiology and Management INTRODUCTION: The Nigeria Field Epidemiology and Laboratory Training Program (NFELTP) is a two-year in-service training program in field epidemiology or veterinary epidemiology or laboratory epidemiology and management. The NFELTP was created to serve as a long-term program within the Federal Ministry of Health (FMOH) and the Federal Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development (FMARD). It trains Field Epidemiologists, Public Health Laboratorians, and Veterinary Epidemiologists for leadership positions in various levels of both the FMOH and the FMARD. The trainees provide epidemiological services to the FMOH, FMARD, State Ministries of Health, and State Ministries of Agriculture and Rural Development during the training, through long-term field placements. The program is currently sponsored by the FMOH and FMARD with funding and technical support of the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). PROGRAM OBJECTIVES: 1. Strengthen capacity to respond to public health emergencies such as outbreaks, epidemics, natural disasters, and emerging and remerging infectious diseases. 2. Strengthen public health and veterinary surveillance systems. 3. Strengthen laboratory capacity and its participation in surveillance and field investigation. 4. Strengthen the linkage between public health and veterinary epidemiology. 5. Conduct research activities on priority public health problems. 6. Improve communications and networking within the country and throughout the region on public health issues. ELIGIBILITY: The NFELTP will focus on training persons who are or will become field epidemiology leaders at Federal, State and Local Government levels. Field epidemiology/public health candidates should have at least • MBBS/M.B.Ch.B, BDS degrees with certification from the Medical and Dental Council of Nigeria (MDCN) • Two years working experience in a related government position (with evidence of confirmation) • Recommendation from the Head of Department/ Ministry • Candidates working with epidemiology and disease control programmes/units at the LGA, State and Federal level programme will have an added advantage • Credits in at least five O level subjects (including English & Mathematics Those interested in the public health laboratory epidemiology and management course should have at least a • BSc degree (with a minimum of second-c lass upper division) in microbiology or relevant subjects. • Registration and Licensing from relevant National council is an added advantage. • Have a minimum of two years’ experience in a government laboratory (with evidence of confirmation). • Candidates working with disease control units at the LGA, State and Federal level programme will have an added advantage • Recommendation from the Head of Department/Ministry • Credits in at least five O’ level subjects, including English and Mathematics. Candidates interested in the MPH Veterinary Epidemiology Practice Course should have at least a • DVM degree with certification from Veterinary Council of Nigeria • Two years working experience within the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development or other relevant State Ministries/Parastatal (with evidence confirmation) • Recommendation from the serving Ministry/Department / Parastatal • Candidates working with disease control units at the LGA, State and Federal level programme will have an added advantage. • Credits in at least five O level subjects (including English & Mathematics ACCEPTABILITY REQUIREMENT: Individuals accepted to the NFELTP will be required to sign a contract committing them to remain in government service for a minimum of five years following graduation. APPLICATION PROCEDURE: The application procedure and form at a fee of N10, 000.00 (and a bank charge of N500.00) will be available online as from the Monday 1st April 2019 to Friday 26th April 2019. The deadline for submission of application is Friday 26th April 2019. Access form on spgs.abu.edu.ng/forms and complete and submit. Incomplete and wrongly filled forms will not be considered. All applicants are advised to read and follow the General Guidelines on the Application Process that has been provided on the portal. These guidelines provide important information about form completion and designated banks where payments can be made. Contact details for technical issues with the website/portal: 08187370686 and 08099926814 After submission, a confirmation message will be sent to the applicant’s email address and telephone. Direct questions may be addressed to the University focal person Dr. Aisha Abubakar (ABU) on 09055092573, e-mail: [email protected] EXAMINATION AND INTERVIEW PROCESS: Shortlisted candidates will be invited for an enrollment examination and will be interviewed by the FELTP National Selection Committee for final recommendation. During the interview, each candidate will be expected to appear with original copies of his/her relevant credentials. In addition, each candidate will be expected to submit his/her academic transcript, formal statement of at least 250 words explaining the candidates educational and career objectives and how these Objectives correspond with the NFELTP, authorization/recommendation from the applicant’s employer, and photocopies of relevant credentials. title: Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention
text: Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention Protecting the health of Nigerians Archive Months Weeks Recent Publication 2019 Field Epidemiology and Laboratory Training Program, Cohort 11, University of Ibadan Monday, April 01, 2019 THE UNIVERSITY OF IBADAN in collaboration with the FEDERAL MINISTRY OF HEALTH (FMOH) AND THE FEDERAL MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE AND RURAL DEVELOPMENT (FMARD) announces admission into the 2018/19 FIELD EPIDEMIOLOGY AND LABORATORY TRAINING PROGRAMME FOR THE AWARD OF: (A) MPH IN FIELD EPIDEMIOLOGY PRACTICE, (B) MPH IN VETERINARY EPIDEMIOLOGY PRACTICE, AND (C) MPH IN LABORATORY EPIDEMIOLOGY PRACTICE INTRODUCTION: The Nigeria Field Epidemiology and Laboratory Training Program (NFELTP) is a two-year in-service training program in Field Epidemiology Practice, Veterinary Epidemiology Practice or Laboratory Epidemiology Practice. The NFELTP was created to serve as a long-term continuing program within the Federal Ministry of Health (FMOH) and the Federal Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development (FMARD). It trains Field Epidemiologists, Public Health Laboratorians, and Veterinary Epidemiologists for leadership positions in various levels of both the Ministry of Health and the Ministry of Agriculture. The trainees provide epidemiological services to the FMOH, State Ministries of Health (SMOH), FMARD and the State Ministries of Agriculture and Rural Development (SMARD), through long-term field placements. The program is currently sponsored by the FMOH and FMARD with f und in g and technical support provided by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). PROGRAM OBJECTIVES • Strengthen capacity to respond to public health emergencies such as outbreaks, epidemics, natural disasters, and emerging and re-emerging infectious diseases • Strengthen public health and veterinary surveillance systems • Strengthen laboratory capacity and its participation in surveillance and field investigation • Strengthen the linkage between public health and veterinary epidemiology • Conduct research activities on priority public health problems • Improve communications and networking within the country and throughout the region on public health issues ELIGIBILITY The NFELTP will focus on training persons who are or will become field epidemiology leaders at Federal, State and LGA levels. A. Candidates interested in the MPH Field Epidemiology Practice course should have at least: - • MBBS/MBChB, BDS degrees with certification from the Medical and Dental Council of Nigeria (MDCN) • Two years working experience in a related government position (with Evidence of confirmation) • Recommendation from the Head of Department/ Ministry • Candidates working with epidemiology and disease control units at the LGA, State and Federal level will have an added advantage B. Candidates interested in the MPH Laboratory Epidemiology Practice course should have at least a • B.Sc. degree (with a minimum of second class upper division) in microbiology or relevant subjects. • Registration and Licensing from relevant National council is an added advantage • Have a minimum of two years working experience in a government laboratory (with evidence of confirmation). • Recommendation from the Head of Department/ Ministry • Candidates working with epidemiology and disease control units at the LGA, State and Federal level will have an added advantage (C) Candidates interested in the MP H Veterinary Epidemiology Practice course should have at least a • DVM degree with certification from Veterinary Council of Nigeria • Two years working experience within the ministry of Agriculture and Rural development or other relevant State Ministries/Parastatal (with evidence confirmation) • Two years working experience within the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural of confirmation) • Recommendation from the Head of Department/ Ministry • Candidates working with epidemiology and disease control units at the LGA, State and Federal level will have an added advantage ACCEPTABILITY REQUIREMENT: I. All candidates must satisfy the matriculation requirements of the University of Ibadan (including required credits in English 'O ‘level exams) as well as the other requirement of the Postgraduate College. Candidates may check the University website for further details. II. Individuals accepted to the NFELTP will be required to sign a contract committing them to remain in government service for a minimum of five years following graduation. APPLICATION PROCEDURE The application procedures and form will be available on the website of the Postgraduate College, University of Ibadan (http://pgcollege.ui.edu.ng/) at a fee. In addition, a fee will be charged for English Proficiency test. The date of the English proficiency test will be communicated. Application procedure will open as from 27th March 2019 to 26th April 2019. The deadline for submission of applications is Friday 26th April 2019. The completed form along with photocopies of relevant credentials, academic transcript and formal statement of at least 250 words explaining the applicant's educational and career objectives and how those objectives correspond with the NFELTP, and authorization/recommendation from the applicant employers should be submitted to the Secretary of the Postgraduate School, University of Ibadan. The PG School requires that all candidates for master’s and diploma programmes TAKE and PASS the English Proficiency test organized by the PG School to be considered for admission. Direct questions to the Ag. Head & NFELTP Focal Person: Dr MD Dairo Tel: 08074074926 Email: [email protected] EXAMINATION AND INTERVIEW PROCESS Shortlisted candidates will be invited for an enrollment interview in May 2019 for final selection by the National Selection Committee consisting of University of Ibadan, Ahmadu Bello University, NCDC/FMOH, FMARD, CDC and African Field Epidemiology Network. Commencement of course: June 2019 Connect Centre Toll Free Number: 6232 Whatsapp: +234 708 71

title: Why exiting Nigeria does not end a company’s tax duties - Businessday NG
text: Saturday, September 19, 2026 X BusinessDay Home Tax Calculator Companies Markets Economy Real Estate Agriculture Aviation Banking Transportation Maritime Legal Business Research post Sports BDFX BD Conferences BD Foundation BusinessDay Intelligence Adverts & Rates About US Our Board Our Management Our Profile Corporate Subscription Home > Economy > Why exiting Nigeria does not end a company’s tax duties Why exiting Nigeria does not end a company’s tax duties Ademide Flower-Olumide September 15, 2026 Share ads Corporate exits do not erase tax obligations Companies may close offices, sell assets, end operations, and even move elsewhere, but exiting Nigeria does not automatically end their tax affairs. Under Nigeria’s new tax administration framework, businesses that cease operations still must file outstanding and final tax returns, raising questions about how tax authorities handle companies after they exit the market. This issue has gained renewed relevance following Uber’s restructuring in Nigeria, highlighting a broader question for multinational companies: what happens to their tax affairs when they leave? Tax expert Nojeem Yusuf explained that a business leaving a country does not conclude its obligations immediately. Companies still need to submit final tax returns, as cessation does not stop outstanding tax liabilities, ongoing disputes, or the authority’s ability to examine corporate affairs. According to the Nigeria Tax Administration Act (NTAA) 2025, any company that permanently ceases trade or business in Nigeria must file tax returns for the cessation year alongside any outstanding returns. Read also: Six months into Nigeria’s tax reforms, businesses demand certainty The law requires companies to file these returns within six months of permanently ceasing operations in Nigeria. Furthermore, if revenue authorities have initiated audits, corporations must remain engaged to resolve those audits and settle any additional tax due. Even without ongoing audits, an exit triggers tax authorities to commence examinations. Managing winding up and related party transactions Shutting down operations is not the final step in a company’s relationship with tax authorities. The NTAA requires every company to designate a representative to manage its tax affairs, running concurrently with the corporate winding-up process governed by the Companies and Allied Matters Act (CAMA) 2020. Writing on the implications of the new law, tax specialist Chizoba Ngwudo noted that insolvency or winding up does not absolve a business of its tax responsibilities. Outstanding liabilities remain collectible from remaining assets and, under specific circumstances, responsible officers. ads ads The tax question becomes more complex when the entity leaving Nigeria is a subsidiary of a multinational group whose parent company continues operations abroad. Although the Nigerian company ceases local operations, transactions between the subsidiary and its foreign parent or related entities remain relevant to the tax authority. This scrutiny is vital when handling outstanding intercompany balances or transferring assets during an exit. Nigeria’s tax framework requires connected transactions to comply with the arm’s length principle, ensuring terms reflect independent market conditions. Related News Two-thirds of Africans oppose more foreign job seekers, refugees – Report AFRICA FINANCE IN BRIEF:Private capital surges as African markets deepen cross border investment Ivory Coast targets 2027 gold refinery start as it seeks top producer spot Read also: Nigeria’s informal economy is more than tax evasion, expert says Tax advisers emphasise that corporate closures and physical shutdowns are separate procedures. Multinationals must distinguish between restructuring, transferring a business to another entity, or formally winding up and dissolving the local company. PwC Nigeria highlights voluntary winding up, deregistration, and striking a company’s name from the Register of Companies as distinct routes for managing exit affairs. Protecting the national revenue base The scale of company income tax collected by the government underscores why departing businesses matter to Nigeria’s revenue base. According to National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) data, Nigeria collected N9.21 trillion in Company Income Tax (CIT) in 2025, representing a 41 percent increase from the previous year. In the first quarter of 2026, CIT collections stood at N1.37 trillion, demonstrating that corporate taxpayers continue to account for a significant pool of government revenue. Foreign CIT payments formed a substantial portion of these collections, reflecting the vital contribution of multinational and non-domestic businesses. ads ads Read also: MAN seeks forex backlog payout, 2025 tax law clarity To ensure full compliance before departure, tax experts recommend a structured action plan: Identify outstanding tax returns and file cessation returns within the six-month statutory period. Reconcile tax records with the revenue authority and properly challenge disputed liabilities within applicable timelines. Review related-party transactions, transfer-pricing documentation, and the treatment of disposed assets as part of the exit strategy. title: Businesses seek joint tax audits as federal, state authorities face coordination gaps - Businessday NG
text: Saturday, September 19, 2026 X BusinessDay Home Tax Calculator Companies Markets Economy Real Estate Agriculture Aviation Banking Transportation Maritime Legal Business Research post Sports BDFX BD Conferences BD Foundation BusinessDay Intelligence Adverts & Rates About US Our Board Our Management Our Profile Corporate Subscription Home > Economy > Businesses seek joint tax audits as federal, state authorities face coordination gaps Businesses seek joint tax audits as federal, state authorities face coordination gaps Ademide Flower-Olumide September 16, 2026 Share ads Businesses are seeking better coordination between federal and state authorities, including joint audits, as stakeholders say overlapping tax engagements remain one of the weak areas in the implementation of Nigeria’s new tax regime. Emeka Chime, tax partner at PwC, said businesses want the Nigeria Revenue Service (NRS) and state authorities to work together more closely to reduce repeated audits and compliance issues. “The law provides a framework for joint audits, and so that is something that tax payers have to see being implemented”, Chime said at the 2026 LCCI-OPS Stakeholders’ Forum on Emerging Tax Matters in Lagos. He emphasised that businesses currently face situations where they may undergo an audit by the NRS and subsequently receive another audit by the Lagos State Internal Revenue Service (LIRS), thereby creating additional compliance demands. This was noted as businesses adjust to the tax reforms that took effect in 2026, with stakeholders at the forum stating that implementation will depend not only on the legislation but also on how easily businesses can comply. ads ads The Executive Chairman of LIRS, represented by Mustafa Foluso, the director of tax audit, said tax reform will succeed better if taxpayers understood the changes, ensures compliance and have confidence in how the system was administered. “Compliance should be made easier, less costly for those willing to comply, while deliberate non compliance should become easier to identify,” he said. He added that technology and data would better shape tax administration by helping authorities understand taxpayers’ behaviour, identify compliance risks and provide more targeted services. Related News Netflix Reviews: Why Did I Get Married The importance of consistent branding across all platforms Top 10 sectors attracting global investment in 2026 The LIRS representative also identified simplification, engagement and collaboration as top key priorities for the next phase of implementation. ads ads Meanwhile, Richard Ayibiowu, president and chairman of the Nigeria Employers’ Consultative Association (NECA), said taxpayers were now embracing their obligations more but still expected clearer benefits from paying taxes. He reflected on the popular Lagos slogan “ Sanwo Ori e, Jaiye lo ” meaning “Pay your tax, enjoy yourself” emphasising that taxpayers were still looking for more in terms of enjoying the benefits of taxation. He said taxpayers were still looking for actual evidence that their tax payments were translating into development and tangible benefits. The Chartered Institute of Directors Nigeria similarly urged continued engagement between government, tax authorities and the private sector, alongside greater use of technology and data to reduce duplication and unnecessary physical interaction. The institute said tax reform should not be judged solely by higher revenue but also by whether it improves compliance, broadens the tax base, and strengthen taxpayer confidence. The forum therefore highlighted an early test for Nigeria’s tax reforms: whether increased revenue and compliance can be matched by a tax system that is clearer, more coordinated, and easier for taxpayers to navigate. Ademide Flower-Olumide Ayomide Odunlami is a Tax Reporter at BusinessDay, covering Nigeria’s tax reforms, compliance trends, and government revenue strategies. She reports on how evolving tax policies affect businesses, investors, and the broader economy, providing clarity on complex regulatory issues through data-driven journalism. title: FirstHoldCo crosses N7trn market cap as FTSE Frontier 50 debut nears - Businessday NG
text: Saturday, September 19, 2026 X BusinessDay Home Tax Calculator Companies Markets Economy Real Estate Agriculture Aviation Banking Transportation Maritime Legal Business Research post Sports BDFX BD Conferences BD Foundation BusinessDay Intelligence Adverts & Rates About US Our Board Our Management Our Profile Corporate Subscription Home > Companies > FirstHoldCo crosses N7trn market cap as FTSE Frontier 50 debut nears FirstHoldCo crosses N7trn market cap as FTSE Frontier 50 debut nears Muhammed Lawal September 18, 2026 Share ads FirstHoldCo Plc, the parent company of FirstBank, crossed the N7 trillion market capitalisation mark on Friday, as its shares rallied ahead of the group’s entry into the FTSE Frontier 50 Index. The financial services group’s shares rose 8.1 percent to N160 from N148, lifting its market value to about N7.28 trillion, based on data from the Nigerian Exchange Limited. The milestone sustains FirstHoldCo lead as the most valuable listed Nigerian bank by market capitalisation, ahead of Zenith Bank and Guaranty Trust Holding Company (GTCO). The rally came on the final trading session before FirstHoldCo’s inclusion in the FTSE Frontier 50 Index, with the revised index taking effect from Monday, September 21. FTSE Russell included FirstHoldCo alongside five other Nigerian companies — Zenith Bank, GTCO, MTN Nigeria, Dangote Cement and Aradel Holdings — in its latest review of the 50-stock frontier-market benchmark. The changes take effect after the close of trading on Friday. ads ads The inclusion coincides with Nigeria’s return to FTSE Russell’s Frontier Market classification, ending a three-year period in which the country was designated Unclassified. FTSE catalyst For FirstHoldCo, the FTSE Frontier 50 inclusion gives the bank greater visibility among global investors and puts its shares within a concentrated benchmark covering 50 companies across frontier markets. The index comprises the largest companies in the broader FTSE Frontier Index universe, subject to requirements including market capitalisation, liquidity, free float and investability. ads ads The timing is significant because the Friday session was the last opportunity for investors to adjust positions before the new index composition becomes effective. Read also: Seplat shares surge 166% as stock nears N15,000 milestone While inclusion does not automatically translate into a specific amount of foreign capital, it can increase demand from investors whose portfolios track or benchmark against the index. FirstHoldCo’s chairman, Femi Otedola, described the inclusion as a “defining milestone” for the group, saying it reflected the transformation of the financial services company and investor confidence in the institution. Otedola’s expanding bet The latest market-cap milestone also adds to the sharp increase in the value of Otedola’s stake in FirstHoldCo. Otedola has spent about N351.2 billion increasing his stake in the financial services group through five disclosed purchases since July 22, according to the transactions disclosed to the market. Related News IGP vows thorough probe into deaths of 37 suspected miners Two-thirds of Africans oppose more foreign job seekers, refugees – Report AFRICA FINANCE IN BRIEF:Private capital surges as African markets deepen cross border investment His latest disclosed acquisition, made through his investment vehicle Calvados Global Services Limited, involved the purchase of 95.7 million FirstHoldCo shares for N12.58 billion on August 24. The purchase took his total holding to about 12.23 billion shares, representing approximately 26.6 percent of FirstHoldCo based on the figures in the company’s disclosures. The chairman’s accumulation has coincided with a sharp appreciation in the bank’s share price, helping to push the group’s market value beyond the N7 trillion threshold. Earnings underpin rally The share-price gains have also come against a backdrop of stronger operating performance. FirstHoldCo reported N526.13 billion in profit after tax for the first half of 2026, while its cost-to-income ratio improved to 44.2 percent. The group has also received shareholder approval for a N253.1 billion capital-raising programme, part of efforts to strengthen its balance sheet and support its growth ambitions. The combination of earnings, capital-raising plans, sustained investor interest and the forthcoming FTSE inclusion has helped reshape the market’s perception of FirstHoldCo. The bank’s valuation milestone is particularly notable given the scale of the recent rally in its shares, which has pushed the company from a market capitalisation of N5 trillion in late July to more than N7 trillion. From N5trn to N7trn FirstHoldCo crossed the N5 trillion market-capitalisation threshold in late July, following Otedola’s increased stake in the group. The latest move means the bank has added more than N2 trillion in market value in a relatively short period, highlighting the extent of the repricing of the stock. The FTSE Frontier 50 inclusion now provides another potential catalyst as FirstHoldCo enters a benchmark followed by international investors. For Nigeria’s capital market, the development also comes at a significant moment. The country’s return to FTSE Russell’s Frontier Market classification restores Nigerian equities to the index provider’s global frontier-market framework after three years of being Unclassified. FTSE Russell said its assessment found no material settlement, operational or funding issues following Nigeria’s transition from T+2 to T+1 settlement. FirstHoldCo’s rise above N7 trillion therefore reflects more than a single day’s share-price gain. It places the bank at the intersection of stronger earnings, increased shareholder accumulation, a major capital-raising programme and renewed international market visibility as Nigeria returns to the global frontier-market universe. title: How investors can legally reduce tax they pay on investments - Businessday NG
text: Saturday, September 19, 2026 X BusinessDay Home Tax Calculator Companies Markets Economy Real Estate Agriculture Aviation Banking Transportation Maritime Legal Business Research post Sports BDFX BD Conferences BD Foundation BusinessDay Intelligence Adverts & Rates About US Our Board Our Management Our Profile Corporate Subscription Home > Economy > How investors can legally reduce tax they pay on investments How investors can legally reduce tax they pay on investments Ayomide Odunlami August 31, 2026 Share ads Nigerians investing in shares, bonds, funds, property, and other assets can legally reduce the tax they pay by taking advantage of exemptions and favourable tax treatments under the country’s new tax regime. The Nigeria Tax Act 2025, which took effect on January 1, 2026, changed the treatment of several forms of investment income and gains, making tax an increasingly important consideration for investors when assessing returns. LessaTax, in an article titled “How Nigerians Can Legally Reduce the Tax They Pay on Their Investments,” highlights several ways investors can structure their investments to take advantage of exemptions and reduce their tax burden while remaining compliant with the law. Read also: How Nigeria is using tax breaks to lure oil investors Government bonds can offer tax-free income ads ads One of the clearest opportunities is in government securities. Income from federal and state government bonds is exempt from tax under the new law, according to an article by Udo Udoma & Belo-Osagie titled ‘Key Tax Incentives Under the Nigeria Tax Act.’ This means investors comparing two investments with similar headline returns may end up with different after-tax amounts depending on the security chosen. For instance, a lower-yielding government bond could deliver a more competitive return after tax than a higher-yielding taxable investment because the bond income is exempt. ads ads The tax treatment should not, however, be the only consideration, as risk, liquidity, and expected return also determine the attractiveness of an investment. Collective investment schemes can also offer tax advantages Investors can also reduce their tax exposure by considering how they invest, not just what they invest in. Collective investment schemes pool money from investors and invest in assets such as shares and bonds. Dividends distributed by authorised collective investment schemes are exempt from income tax under the Nigeria Tax Act. Udo Udoma & Belo-Osagie said the exemption could make collective investment schemes more attractive to retail investors by reducing the tax disadvantage associated with investing through such vehicles. This means investors should consider not only what an investment earns, but also how the income is distributed and taxed. Read also: MAN seeks safeguards for manufacturers under new tax law Foreign investment income comes with conditions Investors earning income from abroad may also benefit from specific exemptions, although these come with conditions. Certain foreign-sourced dividends, interest, rent, and royalties can qualify for exemption where they are brought into Nigeria in convertible currency through approved channels and paid into an approved local bank account, according to PwC. Simply investing abroad, however, does not automatically make the income tax-free. Investors need to meet the conditions attached to the exemption and understand their wider Nigerian tax obligations. Related News IGP vows thorough probe into deaths of 37 suspected miners Two-thirds of Africans oppose more foreign job seekers, refugees – Report AFRICA FINANCE IN BRIEF:Private capital surges as African markets deepen cross border investment Investors selling assets face a different calculation The tax implications become more important when an investor sells an asset at a profit. Under the new regime, individuals no longer pay the former flat 10 percent capital gains tax on chargeable gains. PwC said capital gains for individuals are now taxed at the applicable progressive personal income tax rates. The law nevertheless provides relief for some share disposals. Gains from the disposal of shares can qualify for exemption where the proceeds do not exceed N150 million in any 12 consecutive months, and the attributable gain does not exceed N10 million, according to PwC. Certain proceeds reinvested in shares can also qualify for relief. This makes it important for investors to understand the tax consequences before selling a large portfolio rather than after the transaction has been completed. No withholding tax does not always mean no tax Investors should also distinguish between withholding tax and their final tax liability. The absence of withholding tax on a particular investment income does not automatically mean the income is tax-free. Likewise, tax deducted at source may in some circumstances serve as a credit against the investor’s final liability rather than being the final tax. Understanding the distinction can prevent investors from underestimating what they may eventually owe. Tax planning starts before the investment For investors, tax planning should begin when they are deciding where to put their money, not when the tax bill arrives. A 17 percent return on a taxable investment, for example, cannot be assessed in isolation from a 15 percent return that is exempt from tax. The investor needs to compare what each option actually leaves in their pocket after tax, while also considering the risks involved. The same applies to someone deciding whether to invest directly in securities or through an authorised fund, or an investor holding foreign assets who needs to determine whether the conditions for an exemption have been met. Nigeria’s new tax regime therefore makes after-tax return a more important part of investment decisions. title: Seplat shares surge 166% as stock nears N15,000 milestone - Businessday NG
text: Saturday, September 19, 2026 X BusinessDay Home Tax Calculator Companies Markets Economy Real Estate Agriculture Aviation Banking Transportation Maritime Legal Business Research post Sports BDFX BD Conferences BD Foundation BusinessDay Intelligence Adverts & Rates About US Our Board Our Management Our Profile Corporate Subscription Home > Companies > Seplat shares surge 166% as stock nears N15,000 milestone Seplat shares surge 166% as stock nears N15,000 milestone Muhammed Lawal September 18, 2026 Share ads … Elumelu’s stake gains about N311bn Seplat Energy Plc’s shares have surged 165.9 percent year-to-date to a record N14,907.80, making the oil and gas producer one of the strongest-performing large stocks on the Nigerian market as investors respond to stronger earnings and increased production. The stock gained 10 percent on September 10, rising from N13,552.60 to N14,907.80, according to Nigerian Exchange data, and remained at the record level through September 16. At N14,907.80, Seplat has gained 165.9 percent from N5,610 at the start of 2026 and is up 177.1 percent from N5,379 a year ago. The scale of the rally means investors who held the stock at the beginning of the year have seen the value of their investment more than double, underscoring the strength of the recent re-rating of the company. ads ads The rally has also been mirrored in Seplat’s London listing, where the shares, traded under the ticker SEPL, reached an all-time high of 845 pence on September 16 before closing at 839p. Read also: Seplat crosses N8trn valuation, stock hits 52-week high The London-listed stock subsequently fell 2.7 percent to 816p on September 17, but remained substantially above its 768p level on September 10. Strong earnings provide fundamental support ads ads The sharp appreciation in Seplat’s stock has come alongside a significant improvement in its financial performance. For the six months ended June 2026, the company’s profit before tax increased 74.1 percent year-on-year to N790.4 billion, from N454.1 billion in the corresponding period of last year. Revenue rose 15.5 percent to N2.50 trillion, while production increased to 139,509 barrels of oil equivalent per day. The earnings performance has strengthened the fundamental case for the stock, particularly as Seplat continues to benefit from its expanded production base following the consolidation of its offshore assets. In 2025, the company recorded average group production of 131,506 boepd, while annual revenue reached a record $2.73 billion. The increase in production is important for investors because higher output gives Seplat greater exposure to crude oil prices and provides additional scope for revenue and cash-flow growth. However, the magnitude of the stock’s appreciation has significantly exceeded the growth in revenue and profit, suggesting that market expectations about the company’s future performance are also playing a role in the re-rating. London rally reinforces investor demand Seplat’s performance in London provides another indication of the strength of investor interest in the company. Unlike the Nigerian listing, where the stock has remained at N14,907.80 since September 10, the London-listed shares continued to move higher over subsequent trading sessions. The shares rose from 768p on September 10 to 777p on September 11, 796p on September 14, 822p on September 15 and 839p on September 16, when they briefly touched 845p. Read also: Tony Elumelu’s Seplat stake rises to $1.28 billion as shares gain 8.4% The simultaneous appreciation in both markets suggests that the rally is not simply a function of trading conditions on the Nigerian market. It also gives investors a broader view of how Seplat is being valued internationally, particularly as the company expands its production base and strengthens its position as one of Africa’s significant independent energy producers. Oil prices and geopolitical risks add to the backdrop Global oil-market volatility has provided another important backdrop to the performance of energy stocks. Heightened tensions involving the United States and Iran, alongside uncertainty over vessel traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, have increased volatility in global energy markets. For oil producers, higher crude prices can improve revenue and cash-flow expectations, although the effect depends on realised prices, production levels, costs, hedging and other factors. Seplat’s stock performance should therefore not be attributed to oil prices alone. The company’s stronger production, earnings growth and expanded asset base provide company-specific drivers, while movements in global crude markets influence the broader valuation environment for energy producers. Read also: Nigerian tycoon Tony Elumelu set to earn another $14.45m from Seplat Energy dividend Elumelu’s stake gains about N311bn The rally has also significantly increased the value of major shareholder holdings. Tony Elumelu’s indirect 120.4 million-share stake, held through Heirs Energies and Heirs Holdings, was worth about N1.48 trillion when Seplat traded at N12,320.60 on September 1. At the current record price of N14,907.80, the holding is worth approximately N1.79 trillion. That represents an increase of about N311.5 billion in the value of the stake in just over two weeks. The increase illustrates the wealth effect of Seplat’s rally for its major shareholders and shows how quickly changes in the stock price can translate into large movements in the value of strategic holdings. title: Sterling Holdings reshuffles board, appoints former Ecobank risk chief - Businessday NG
text: Saturday, September 19, 2026 X BusinessDay Home Tax Calculator Companies Markets Economy Real Estate Agriculture Aviation Banking Transportation Maritime Legal Business Research post Sports BDFX BD Conferences BD Foundation BusinessDay Intelligence Adverts & Rates About US Our Board Our Management Our Profile Corporate Subscription Home > Companies > Sterling Holdings reshuffles board, appoints former Ecobank risk chief Sterling Holdings reshuffles board, appoints former Ecobank risk chief Muhammed Lawal September 18, 2026 Share ads Sterling Financial Holdings Company Plc has appointed Laoye Jaiyeola and Chinedu Ikwudinma as independent non-executive directors of Sterling Bank Limited, following the retirement of three directors at the expiration of their tenure. The Nigerian banking group also announced the retirement of Tunde Adeola, an executive director of Sterling Bank, after he attained the prescribed retirement age. The changes were disclosed in a statement on Wednesday signed by Sunny Kanabe, company secretary of the group. The retiring directors are Michael Ajukwu, Olusola Oworu and Olaitan Kajero, who left the board following the expiration of their respective tenures. The board expressed its appreciation to the retiring directors “for their dedication, leadership and contributions to the growth of the group” and wished them success in their future endeavours. ads ads Jaiyeola brings 35 years of financial services experience Jaiyeola joins the board with more than 35 years of experience spanning financial services, corporate governance and public policy in Nigeria. He spent nearly two decades at the Central Bank of Nigeria and later served as managing director and CEO of Kakawa Discount House Limited, now Quest Merchant Bank. He has held several senior leadership and board positions, including president of the Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria and chief executive officer of the Nigerian Economic Summit Group. ads ads Jaiyeola currently serves on the board of FMDQ Group Plc, the NESG Advisory Board and the Policy Innovation Centre. He holds a B.Sc. in Economics from Obafemi Awolowo University, a master’s degree in Banking and Finance from the University of Lagos and an MBA from Bangor University. He is a Fellow of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of Nigeria, the Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria and the Chartered Institute of Directors. He is also a Chartered Member of the Chartered Banker Institute, Scotland. Related News Netflix Reviews: Why Did I Get Married The importance of consistent branding across all platforms Top 10 sectors attracting global investment in 2026 Jaiyeola is a Senior Executive Fellow of Harvard Kennedy School and founder and pro-chancellor of Hillside University of Science and Technology. Ikwudinma brings Ecobank, Citibank experience Ikwudinma was appointed an independent non-executive director of Sterling Bank effective August 20, 2026. He brings more than three decades of international banking and financial services experience, spanning risk management, corporate and investment banking, commercial banking, transaction banking, strategic leadership and governance across African and global markets. He spent more than two decades with Citibank, holding senior leadership positions in Nigeria, Zambia and Uganda. Ikwudinma served as managing director and chief executive officer of Citibank Uganda and as executive director and country risk manager for Citibank Nigeria. He most recently served as group chief risk officer of Ecobank Transnational Incorporated, having previously served as the group’s chief credit officer. Before joining Ecobank, he was the pioneer managing director of Nova Merchant Bank Limited. He currently serves as chairman of CS&C Associates Limited. Ikwudinma holds a Bachelor of Engineering degree in Civil Engineering from the University of Nigeria, Nsukka, an M.Sc. in Structural Engineering and an MBA in Finance from the University of Lagos. He is a Fellow of the Nigerian Institute of Credit Administration and a Member of the Institute of Directors. The appointments strengthen Sterling Bank’s board with additional expertise in risk management, credit, financial services, corporate governance and international banking as the lender continues to execute its growth strategy. title: How Nigerian, South African lenders are rewriting Africa’s banking M&A playbook - Businessday NG
text: Saturday, September 19, 2026 X BusinessDay Home Tax Calculator Companies Markets Economy Real Estate Agriculture Aviation Banking Transportation Maritime Legal Business Research post Sports BDFX BD Conferences BD Foundation BusinessDay Intelligence Adverts & Rates About US Our Board Our Management Our Profile Corporate Subscription Home > Africa > How Nigerian, South African lenders are rewriting Africa’s banking M&A playbook How Nigerian, South African lenders are rewriting Africa’s banking M&A playbook Bunmi Bailey September 18, 2026 Share ads Nigerian and South African banks are taking increasingly different approaches to expansion across Africa, with Nigerian lenders favouring a series of acquisitions while South African groups are placing fewer but significantly larger controlling bets, a new report shows. The divergence is emerging as cross-border banking mergers and acquisitions accelerate across East Africa, with Kenya attracting the greatest deal value and Tanzania developing as a secondary market for banks seeking to build regional platforms. The M&A Trends in East Africa Banking Sector report by Deals & Advisory Report tracks six major banking transactions between 2024 and mid-2026 and identifies four acquiring banking groups. Nigerian and South African banks are the dominant acquirers, with most transactions targeting between 66 percent and 100 percent ownership, giving buyers control over operations and greater freedom to integrate businesses. “Almost every deal targets 66 to 100 percent ownership — buyers want operational control and integration freedom,” the report said. ads ads “Kenya is the clear centre of gravity, with Tanzania as a secondary platform-building market. Nigerian banks, led by Access Bank and followed by Zenith, have pursued volume through sequential deals, while South Africa’s Nedbank placed one large controlling bet on NCBA Group, the region’s flagship transaction at roughly $856 million.” Read also: Angola cuts rates to lowest since 2016 as inflation hits single digit The contrasting strategies point to a broader shift in African banking M&A: banks are increasingly buying capabilities, licences, customer relationships and distribution networks rather than simply adding assets to their balance sheets. Nigeria’s volume strategy Access Bank has emerged as the most active Nigerian acquirer in the region, according to the report. ads ads Its transactions include the acquisition of National Bank of Kenya, BancABC Tanzania and Standard Chartered’s consumer, private and business banking business in Tanzania. The National Bank of Kenya transaction was valued at about KSh15.8 billion, or roughly $100 million-$110 million, while in Tanzania, Access used BancABC as a platform before adding Standard Chartered’s banking relationships and capabilities. Zenith Bank has followed a similar strategy, including its acquisition of Paramount Bank in Tanzania for more than $7.7 million. The strategy allows Nigerian banks to build regional footprints through multiple transactions, adding markets and capabilities incrementally rather than relying on a single transformational acquisition. The approach is partly supported by the capital Nigerian banks have raised following the Central Bank of Nigeria’s recapitalisation exercise. Nigerian banks raised more than N4.65 trillion in fresh capital to meet new minimum capital requirements, giving some lenders additional capacity to pursue expansion at home and across the continent. Access Bank became the first lender to exceed its new capital threshold after raising N351 billion ($242 million) through a rights issue. Speaking during the group’s 2024 investor call, Roosevelt Ogbonna, group managing director of Access Bank, said the capital raise was designed to fund expansion rather than simply meet regulatory requirements. “We have consistently stated that our capital raise had nothing to do with the Central Bank’s directive requiring banks to raise their minimum capital,” Ogbonna said. “The capital was deployed immediately, and its impact is already visible.” A significant portion of the proceeds financed the acquisition of Standard Chartered’s subsidiaries in Angola, Sierra Leone, Tanzania and The Gambia, alongside National Bank of Kenya and a majority stake in Mauritius-based AfrAsia Bank. The acquisitions have helped strengthen Access’s position as one of Africa’s most geographically diversified banking groups. The expansion is already changing the group’s earnings profile. Nigeria’s contribution to Access Holdings’ pre-tax profit fell to 37 percent between January and September 2025, from 61 percent two years earlier, while African subsidiaries nearly doubled their contribution to 35 percent. The UK and other international businesses accounted for the remaining 28 percent. Zenith Bank is pursuing a similar internationalisation strategy. The bank, which recently completed a capital raise of more than N350 billion ($242 million), has set an ambitious target of generating about half of its profits outside Nigeria over the medium term. Related News IGP vows thorough probe into deaths of 37 suspected miners Two-thirds of Africans oppose more foreign job seekers, refugees – Report AFRICA FINANCE IN BRIEF:Private capital surges as African markets deepen cross border investment South Africa bets bigger South Africa’s approach is more concentrated. Nedbank agreed to acquire about 66 percent of Kenya-based NCBA Group in a transaction valued at roughly $855 million-$856 million, making it the largest pure banking transaction covered in the report. Rather than building its East African presence through a series of smaller acquisitions, Nedbank is using one major transaction to gain immediate scale across multiple markets. The deal would give the South African lender an East African platform spanning Kenya, Rwanda, Tanzania and Uganda, while combining Nedbank’s corporate and investment banking capabilities with NCBA’s digital and retail reach.

title: Seplat shares surge 166% as stock nears N15,000 milestone - Businessday NG
text: Saturday, September 19, 2026 X BusinessDay Home Tax Calculator Companies Markets Economy Real Estate Agriculture Aviation Banking Transportation Maritime Legal Business Research post Sports BDFX BD Conferences BD Foundation BusinessDay Intelligence Adverts & Rates About US Our Board Our Management Our Profile Corporate Subscription Home > Companies > Seplat shares surge 166% as stock nears N15,000 milestone Seplat shares surge 166% as stock nears N15,000 milestone Muhammed Lawal September 18, 2026 Share ads Seplat Energy Plc’s shares have surged 165.9 percent year-to-date to a record N14,907.80, making the oil and gas producer one of the strongest-performing large stocks on the Nigerian market as investors respond to stronger earnings and increased production. The stock gained 10 percent on September 10, rising from N13,552.60 to N14,907.80, according to Nigerian Exchange data, and remained at the record level through September 16. At N14,907.80, Seplat has gained 165.9 percent from N5,610 at the start of 2026 and is up 177.1 percent from N5,379 a year ago. The scale of the rally means investors who held the stock at the beginning of the year have seen the value of their investment more than double, underscoring the strength of the recent re-rating of the company. The rally has also been mirrored in Seplat’s London listing, where the shares, traded under the ticker SEPL, reached an all-time high of 845 pence on September 16 before closing at 839p. ads ads The London-listed stock subsequently fell 2.7 percent to 816p on September 17, but remained substantially above its 768p level on September 10. Strong earnings provide fundamental support The sharp appreciation in Seplat’s stock has come alongside a significant improvement in its financial performance. For the six months ended June 2026, the company’s profit before tax increased 74.1 percent year-on-year to N790.4 billion, from N454.1 billion in the corresponding period of last year. Revenue rose 15.5 percent to N2.50 trillion, while production increased to 139,509 barrels of oil equivalent per day. ads ads The earnings performance has strengthened the fundamental case for the stock, particularly as Seplat continues to benefit from its expanded production base following the consolidation of its offshore assets. In 2025, the company recorded average group production of 131,506 boepd, while annual revenue reached a record $2.73 billion. The increase in production is important for investors because higher output gives Seplat greater exposure to crude oil prices and provides additional scope for revenue and cash-flow growth. However, the magnitude of the stock’s appreciation has significantly exceeded the growth in revenue and profit, suggesting that market expectations about the company’s future performance are also playing a role in the re-rating. London rally reinforces investor demand Seplat’s performance in London provides another indication of the strength of investor interest in the company. Related News Two-thirds of Africans oppose more foreign job seekers, refugees – Report AFRICA FINANCE IN BRIEF:Private capital surges as African markets deepen cross border investment Ivory Coast targets 2027 gold refinery start as it seeks top producer spot Unlike the Nigerian listing, where the stock has remained at N14,907.80 since September 10, the London-listed shares continued to move higher over subsequent trading sessions. The shares rose from 768p on September 10 to 777p on September 11, 796p on September 14, 822p on September 15 and 839p on September 16, when they briefly touched 845p. The simultaneous appreciation in both markets suggests that the rally is not simply a function of trading conditions on the Nigerian market. It also gives investors a broader view of how Seplat is being valued internationally, particularly as the company expands its production base and strengthens its position as one of Africa’s significant independent energy producers. Oil prices and geopolitical risks add to the backdrop Global oil-market volatility has provided another important backdrop to the performance of energy stocks. Heightened tensions involving the United States and Iran, alongside uncertainty over vessel traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, have increased volatility in global energy markets. For oil producers, higher crude prices can improve revenue and cash-flow expectations, although the effect depends on realised prices, production levels, costs, hedging and other factors. Seplat’s stock performance should therefore not be attributed to oil prices alone. The company’s stronger production, earnings growth and expanded asset base provide company-specific drivers, while movements in global crude markets influence the broader valuation environment for energy producers. Elumelu’s stake gains about N311bn The rally has also significantly increased the value of major shareholder holdings. Tony Elumelu’s indirect 120.4 million-share stake, held through Heirs Energies and Heirs Holdings, was worth about N1.48 trillion when Seplat traded at N12,320.60 on September 1. At the current record price of N14,907.80, the holding is worth approximately N1.79 trillion. That represents an increase of about N311.5 billion in the value of the stake in just over two weeks. The increase illustrates the wealth effect of Seplat’s rally for its major shareholders and shows how quickly changes in the stock price can translate into large movements in the value of strategic holdings. title: Angola cuts rates to lowest since 2016 as inflation hits single digit - Businessday NG
text: Saturday, September 19, 2026 X BusinessDay Home Tax Calculator Companies Markets Economy Real Estate Agriculture Aviation Banking Transportation Maritime Legal Business Research post Sports BDFX BD Conferences BD Foundation BusinessDay Intelligence Adverts & Rates About US Our Board Our Management Our Profile Corporate Subscription Home > Africa > Angola cuts rates to lowest since 2016 as inflation hits single digit Angola cuts rates to lowest since 2016 as inflation hits single digit Faith Omoboye September 18, 2026 Share ads Angola’s central bank has cut its key interest rate by 100 basis points to 14.75 percent, its third consecutive reduction, as inflation fell to single digits for the first time in more than a decade. The National Bank of Angola lowered its policy rate from 15.75 percent at its September 2026 meeting on Tuesday, taking the benchmark to its lowest level since 2016 as price pressures continued to ease and economic growth strengthened. Inflation fell to 8.78 percent year on year in August from 9.33 percent in July, extending a downward trend that began in mid 2024. It was the lowest inflation rate recorded in Angola since April 2015. The central bank maintained its year end inflation forecast at 8.6 percent, suggesting that policymakers expect price pressures to continue easing despite uncertainty created by the conflict in the Middle East. The latest rate cut follows a 125 basis point reduction in July and a 50 basis point cut in May, bringing the total reduction in the policy rate this year to 275 basis points. ads ads The central bank also raised its economic growth forecast for 2026 sharply to 6.15 percent from 3.6 percent previously, citing stronger performance in both the oil and non-oil sectors. Official data showed the economy expanded 8.74 percent year on year in the second quarter, up from 5.32 percent in the first quarter and marking its strongest growth since the second quarter of 2022. The improved outlook comes as Angola benefits from higher global energy prices, although policymakers remain alert to risks from the conflict in the Middle East and its impact on shipping, energy costs and imported goods. Related News Two-thirds of Africans oppose more foreign job seekers, refugees – Report AFRICA FINANCE IN BRIEF:Private capital surges as African markets deepen cross border investment Ivory Coast targets 2027 gold refinery start as it seeks top producer spot Manuel Tiago Dias, governor of the National Bank of Angola, said inflation was still expected to end the year at 8.6 percent. ads ads The easing inflation environment gives the central bank more room to reduce borrowing costs while supporting economic activity, although the pace of further cuts will depend on how prices, the exchange rate and external conditions develop. Liandra da Silva, an economist at Nedbank, told Reuters that Angola’s position as an oil exporter provided some protection against external shocks, but warned that higher shipping costs and imported input prices could still add to inflation. Angola’s stronger oil revenues have also drawn attention to how the government manages the additional income. The International Monetary Fund has urged the government to use oil revenue windfalls to reduce debt and build fiscal buffers rather than allowing higher oil earnings to translate into greater spending. Vera Daves de Sousa, Angola’s Finance Minister, told Reuters last week that the government was likely to raise its 2027 oil price assumption from the $61 per barrel used in this year’s budget, while maintaining a conservative approach to its forecasts. For the central bank, the combination of falling inflation and stronger economic growth provides a more favourable environment for monetary easing. However, external risks remain, particularly if higher energy prices and transport costs feed into imported inflation.
